task.situation: ‘Earthwise Youth’, an online magazine for young people who care about the environment, is holding an essay competition. This year’s question is: ‘Is second-hand the answer to fast fashion?’ The winning essays will appear on the magazine’s website, and you have decided to take part.
points: explain why second-hand clothes have become popular with young people
discuss the limits of second-hand shopping
evaluate other ways in which consumers can reduce the impact of fast fashion

words.long: Give your essay a title. Write around 400 words.

task.de: Ein Essay für den Wettbewerb eines Umweltmagazins für Jugendliche: Ist Secondhand die Antwort auf Fast Fashion? Drei Inhaltspunkte: warum Secondhand bei Jugendlichen beliebt ist, wo seine Grenzen liegen, welche anderen Möglichkeiten Konsument:innen haben. Zuerst wählt ihr eure Position, der Titel kommt ganz zum Schluss.

focus.label: impersonal phrases
focus.note: Marked: impersonal phrases that replace ‘I think’ or ‘we should’: openers with It or There (It could be argued that …, There is a real danger that …) and passive forms with a modal verb (… cannot be expected, … should be encouraged).

steps.q: ‘Is second-hand the answer to fast fashion?’ What is our position?
steps.de: Zuerst entscheidet ihr euch für eine Position, nach der sich das ganze Essay richtet.

options.label: Yes
options.teaser: Buying second-hand is the most effective thing consumers can do against fast fashion.

options.label: No
options.teaser: Second-hand helps, but as long as so many new clothes are made, it cannot solve the problem.

options.label: Partly
options.teaser: Second-hand is an important part of the answer, but only together with buying less and other new habits.

steps.q: How do we introduce the topic and state our thesis?
steps.de: Die Einleitung führt in die Frage des Essays ein. Prüft jede Option: Aufgabe, Aufbau, Wortschatz, Grammatik.
steps.own: Copy the frame. Then finish the introduction in your own words and end with a clear thesis statement.
steps.ownDe: Gerüst abschreiben, dann die Einleitung mit eigenen Worten fertigschreiben. Am Ende steht eure These (Thesis Statement).

options.label: Start with the problem
options.why: Describes the problem and the trend in three short sentences, then the thesis names our position.

map.yes: {{Fast fashion has changed the way people buy clothes.}} New collections arrive constantly at low prices, and [[it is hardly surprising that]] many garments are worn only a few times. At the same time, second-hand shops are attracting young customers. {{This essay will argue that}} buying used clothes is the most effective step consumers can take against this culture of constant buying.
map.no: {{Fast fashion has changed the way people buy clothes.}} New collections arrive constantly at low prices, and [[it is hardly surprising that]] many garments are worn only a few times. At the same time, second-hand shops are attracting young customers. {{This essay will argue that}} this trend, welcome as it is, [[cannot be expected]] to solve the problem on its own.
map.partly: {{Fast fashion has changed the way people buy clothes.}} New collections arrive constantly at low prices, and [[it is hardly surprising that]] many garments are worn only a few times. At the same time, second-hand shops are attracting young customers. {{This essay will argue that}} this trend is part of the answer but [[must be combined]] with other changes in buying habits.

options.label: Start with a contrast
options.why: Two opposite trends and a question make the issue interesting before the thesis gives the answer.

map.yes: {{Never before have clothes been so cheap and so easy to replace.}} Yet second-hand shops are attracting more and more young customers. Can a trend like this really slow down a whole industry? {{This essay will argue that it can,}} as [[it is clear that]] buying used clothes is the most effective way for consumers to reduce the damage done by fast fashion.
map.no: {{Never before have clothes been so cheap and so easy to replace.}} Yet second-hand shops are attracting more and more young customers, and [[it is often claimed that]] this trend will solve the problem. Can buying used clothes really stop an industry that keeps growing? {{This essay will argue that it cannot,}} since new clothes keep flooding the market at the same time.
map.partly: {{Never before have clothes been so cheap and so easy to replace.}} Yet second-hand shops are attracting more and more young customers. Can such a trend really change the way clothes are produced? {{This essay will argue that}} it is a real step forward, although [[it is clear that]] it can only succeed if consumers also change other habits, such as how often they shop.

steps.q: Body paragraph 1 (content point 1): why has second-hand become popular with young people?
steps.de: Der erste Hauptteil knüpft an den Trend aus der Einleitung an und nennt Gründe. Prüft jede Option: Aufgabe, Aufbau, Wortschatz, Grammatik.
steps.own: Copy the frame. Then explain each reason in your own words and give an example of your own.
steps.ownDe: Gerüst abschreiben, dann jeden Grund mit eigenen Worten erklären und ein eigenes Beispiel nennen.

options.label: Price and style
options.why: The impersonal topic sentence picks up the trend from the introduction; price, style and a social side follow with examples.
options.text: {{[[There are several reasons why]] second-hand clothing has won over so many young people.}} The most obvious one is price: a flea-market jacket often costs less than a cinema ticket, which matters to anyone living on pocket money or a part-time wage. Just as important is style. {{Used clothes allow people to wear something}} that nobody else in their class owns, and [[it is no coincidence that]] pieces from earlier decades are fashionable again. {{Shopping for them has become}} a social activity as well: friends visit flea markets together and compare their finds afterwards.

options.label: Apps and values
options.why: ‘The second-hand trend’ links back to the introduction; technology and values follow, each with a detail.
options.text: {{Two recent developments help to explain the second-hand trend.}} The first is technology: resale apps allow clothes to be bought and sold in a few minutes, without a trip to a shop, and a photo taken with a phone is enough to find a buyer. {{The second is a change in values.}} Many young people care about the planet, and [[it is widely accepted that]] reusing clothes saves the water, energy and raw materials needed to make new ones. {{For many of them, buying a used jumper is}} a small but visible way of acting on these beliefs.

options.label: Prices, apps and the planet
options.text: Second-hand clothes are popular with young people because they are much cheaper as new ones. A pair of jeans from a flea market often costs only a few euros, and students with little money can afford more interesting clothes. On resale apps, old clothes can be sold in a few minutes, what makes shopping very easy. Many teenagers also worry about the environment because far too many clothes land in the rubbish every year, often after being worn only once or twice. For them, buying used clothes is a simple way to do something about it.
options.reject: Three typical mistakes: ‘cheaper as’ (→ cheaper than), ‘what makes shopping very easy’ (→ which makes) and ‘land in the rubbish’ (→ end up in the rubbish).
options.rejectDe: Drei typische Fehler: cheaper as → cheaper than, what → which, land in (landen) → end up in.

steps.q: Body paragraph 2 (content point 2): where are the limits of second-hand shopping, and what does the other side say?
steps.de: Der zweite Hauptteil wendet sich von den Gründen zu den Grenzen von Secondhand und nimmt ein Gegenargument auf. Prüft jede Option: Aufgabe, Aufbau, Wortschatz, Grammatik.
steps.own: Copy the frame. Then explain the limits of second-hand shopping in your own words and answer the objection.
steps.ownDe: Gerüst abschreiben, dann die Grenzen von Secondhand mit eigenen Worten erklären und auf den Einwand antworten.

options.label: Limits and the shopping scene
options.text: Second-hand shopping has clear limits. Many donated clothes are in poor condition, and large amounts of used clothing are shipped abroad, where much of it ends up on rubbish tips. Resale apps, however, have made selling old clothes very easy, as a photo taken with a phone is enough to find a buyer within minutes. Flea markets are also popular places to meet friends at the weekend. Vintage pieces from earlier decades have become fashionable again, and many young people enjoy wearing something that nobody else owns. Low prices are another advantage for students who live on pocket money.
options.reject: The topic sentence announces the limits, but after one example the paragraph drifts back to why second-hand is popular (apps, flea markets, vintage, prices). Every sentence must support the topic sentence.
options.rejectDe: Der Topic Sentence kündigt die Grenzen an, doch nach einem Beispiel kehrt der Absatz zu den Gründen für die Beliebtheit zurück (Apps, Flohmärkte, Vintage, Preise). Jeder Satz muss den Topic Sentence stützen.

options.label: Too many, too poor
options.why: ‘It must be admitted’ turns from the reasons to the limits; two concrete problems and an answer to the objection follow.

map.yes: {{Second-hand shopping, [[it must be admitted]], has its limits.}} Many fast-fashion items wear out so quickly that they are hardly worth reselling, and large amounts of donated clothing are shipped abroad, where much of it is simply thrown away. {{These problems are real, but they [[can be reduced]]}} if durable clothes are bought and resold locally. {{[[It could even be argued that]]}} second-hand shopping changes nothing, as fast-fashion labels continue to produce as much as before. {{Companies, after all, only produce what they can sell,}} and if demand for new clothes falls, production [[will be cut]] sooner or later.
map.no: {{Second-hand shopping, [[it must be admitted]], has its limits.}} Many fast-fashion items wear out so quickly that they are hardly worth reselling, and large amounts of donated clothing are shipped abroad, where much of it is simply thrown away. {{[[It follows that]]}} an ever-growing mountain of cheap clothes [[cannot be absorbed]] by second-hand trade alone. {{[[It could be argued that]]}} companies only produce what people are willing to buy. {{This is true in theory, but}} second-hand shops cannot supply everything, from underwear to sports kit, and most shoppers will keep buying new items for these needs.
map.partly: {{Second-hand shopping, [[it must be admitted]], has its limits.}} Many fast-fashion items wear out so quickly that they are hardly worth reselling, and large amounts of donated clothing are shipped abroad, where much of it is simply thrown away. {{[[It follows that]]}} second-hand only works well when clothes are made to last in the first place. {{[[It could be argued that]]}} such limits make second-hand shopping pointless. {{This view [[cannot be accepted]]:}} every used garment that replaces a new one reduces demand a little, and small changes add up when millions of shoppers make them.

options.label: Buying more, not less
options.why: ‘Yet this popularity’ links back to Body paragraph 1, points out a less obvious limit and deals with the other side.

map.yes: {{Yet this popularity has a less obvious downside: its effect on shopping habits.}} Bargains tempt some people to buy more, and selling old outfits online can even become a way to pay for new ones. {{[[It should be remembered that]]}} such cases are the exception: for most buyers, a used jacket simply replaces a new one. {{Critics also point out that}} used clothes are not always available in the right size. {{[[It is true that]]}} the search can take time, but filters in resale apps have made it much easier than it was a few years ago.
map.no: {{Yet this popularity has a less obvious downside: its effect on shopping habits.}} Bargains tempt some people to buy more, and selling old outfits online can even become a way to pay for new ones. {{[[There is a real danger that]]}} second-hand turns into just another form of fast fashion, with clothes changing owners faster and faster. {{Optimists point out that}} if millions of people stopped buying new clothes, the industry would have to change. {{[[It is true that]] this works in theory,}} but only if almost everyone takes part, which seems unrealistic as long as new clothes cost so little.
map.partly: {{Yet this popularity has a less obvious downside: its effect on shopping habits.}} Bargains tempt some people to buy more, and selling old outfits online can even become a way to pay for new ones. {{[[It is therefore essential that]]}} second-hand bargains do not become an excuse to shop more often. {{Some critics would argue that}} only a complete boycott of fast fashion would help. {{[[It is true that]]}} small steps can seem frustrating. {{In reality, a boycott [[could hardly be organised]]}} on a large scale, whereas second-hand shopping is already part of many people’s everyday lives.

steps.q: Body paragraph 3 (content point 3): what else can consumers do, and how useful is it?
steps.de: Der dritte Hauptteil geht über Secondhand hinaus und bewertet andere Möglichkeiten der Konsument:innen. Prüft jede Option: Aufgabe, Aufbau, Wortschatz, Grammatik.
steps.own: Copy the frame. Then evaluate the options in your own words: which one works best, and why?
steps.ownDe: Gerüst abschreiben, dann die Möglichkeiten mit eigenen Worten bewerten: Was funktioniert am besten, und warum?

options.label: Compare the options
options.why: ‘Several other ways’ moves on from second-hand; the options are named and then evaluated, as ‘evaluate’ asks.

map.yes: {{Consumers have several other ways to reduce the effects of fast fashion.}} Swapping works well among friends, repairing keeps favourite pieces in use, and borrowing is ideal for special occasions such as a school-leavers’ ball. {{[[It is evident, however, that]]}} none of these is as practical for everyday clothing as buying second-hand. {{Local initiatives make such habits easier:}} clothes swaps at schools and flea markets in town halls show how quickly used clothing can find new owners. {{Such events [[should be supported]] by councils,}} as habits formed at a young age often last a lifetime.
map.no: {{Consumers have several other ways to reduce the effects of fast fashion.}} Swapping works well among friends, repairing keeps favourite pieces in use, and borrowing is ideal for special occasions such as a school-leavers’ ball. {{[[It must be remembered, however, that]]}} all of these options only deal with clothes that have already been produced. {{Local initiatives make such habits easier:}} clothes swaps at schools and flea markets in town halls show how quickly used clothing can find new owners. {{A busy flea market, though, [[should not be mistaken]]}} for a sign that fewer new clothes are being made.
map.partly: {{Consumers have several other ways to reduce the effects of fast fashion.}} Swapping works well among friends, repairing keeps favourite pieces in use, and borrowing is ideal for special occasions such as a school-leavers’ ball. {{[[It is often forgotten, however, that]]}} the most effective option is simply to buy fewer clothes and wear them for longer. {{Local initiatives make such habits easier:}} clothes swaps at schools and flea markets in town halls show how quickly used clothing can find new owners. {{Such events [[should be extended]],}} but [[it seems unlikely that]] volunteers can keep them going without help from councils.

options.label: Swap, repair, borrow
options.text: Consumers have several other ways to deal with fast fashion. At clothes swaps, people bring items they no longer wear and take home something else in return. Repair cafés are run by volunteers who show visitors how to sew on buttons, mend holes or replace zips. For special occasions such as a school-leavers’ ball, dresses and suits can be borrowed from friends or hired from rental services. Some towns also organise monthly flea markets in schools or town halls, where families sell clothes that their children have grown out of.
options.reject: The task says ‘evaluate’, but this paragraph only describes how swaps, repair cafés and rentals work. It never says how useful they are or compares them with second-hand shopping, so content point 3 is not really covered.
options.rejectDe: Die Aufgabe verlangt „evaluate“, doch der Absatz beschreibt nur, wie Tauschbörsen, Reparaturcafés und Verleih funktionieren. Er bewertet nichts und vergleicht nichts mit Secondhand.

options.label: Care and pressure on producers
options.why: Weighs two overlooked options against second-hand shopping.

map.yes: {{Beyond second-hand shopping, two options are often overlooked: caring for clothes and putting pressure on producers.}} Washing at lower temperatures and mending small holes can make a garment last much longer. {{[[It cannot be denied that]]}} this takes time and some skill, but combined with second-hand shopping, it keeps clothes in use for many years. {{Pressure on producers works on a larger scale.}} The European Union has recently stopped large companies from destroying unsold clothes, and [[it seems likely that]] such rules [[would be tightened]] faster if more shoppers showed, by buying second-hand, that they want change.
map.no: {{Beyond second-hand shopping, two options are often overlooked: caring for clothes and putting pressure on producers.}} Washing at lower temperatures and mending small holes can make a garment last much longer. {{[[There is much to be said for]]}} this habit, as a jacket that is worn for ten years does not need replacing, whether it was bought new or used. {{Pressure on producers works on a larger scale,}} for instance when consumers support stricter rules. {{This is where the biggest difference [[can be made]]:}} a single rule for producers affects millions of garments at once, far more than any shopping decision.
map.partly: {{Beyond second-hand shopping, two options are often overlooked: caring for clothes and putting pressure on producers.}} Washing at lower temperatures and mending small holes can make a garment last much longer. {{[[It seems reasonable to conclude that]]}} caring for clothes and buying second-hand work best together, as both keep garments out of the bin for longer. {{Pressure on producers works on a larger scale.}} The European Union has recently stopped large companies from destroying unsold clothes, and [[it is likely that]] such rules and second-hand shopping will support each other: one discourages overproduction, the other keeps existing clothes in use.

steps.q: How do we end the essay?
steps.de: Der Schluss greift These und Hauptteile auf und rundet das Essay ab. Prüft jede Option: Aufgabe, Aufbau, Wortschatz, Grammatik.
steps.own: Copy the frame. Then sum up our position and the three body paragraphs in two or three sentences of your own.
steps.ownDe: Gerüst abschreiben, dann unsere Position und die drei Body Paragraphs in zwei bis drei eigenen Sätzen zusammenfassen.

options.label: Sum up the position
options.why: Picks up the thesis and the three body paragraphs one by one, without ‘I think’.

map.yes: {{In conclusion, [[it is fair to say that]]}} second-hand shopping is the best answer consumers have to fast fashion. Young people have good reasons to choose it. Its limits are real but smaller than its benefits, and it works even better alongside other ways of keeping clothes in use. {{For this reason, it [[should be encouraged]]}} wherever possible.
map.no: {{In conclusion, [[it is fair to say that]]}} second-hand shopping is a popular and welcome trend among young people. {{Its limits are too great to ignore:}} as long as new clothes are so cheap, second-hand trade cannot keep up with them. {{Other habits help as well, but}} real change [[can only be achieved]] by making far fewer new garments.
map.partly: {{In conclusion, [[it is fair to say that]]}} second-hand shopping is popular for good reasons and makes a real contribution against fast fashion. Given its limits, it [[cannot be relied on]] alone. {{It works best alongside other habits:}} buying fewer clothes, caring for them and passing them on when they are no longer needed.

options.label: Weigh up the arguments
options.why: ‘On balance’ shows that the verdict grows out of the reasons, limits and alternatives discussed.

map.yes: {{On balance, [[it would appear that]]}} the most sustainable garment is one that already exists. Second-hand shopping turns this idea into everyday practice, and its popularity among young people shows that it works on a large scale. {{Its weak points are real}} but manageable. {{It [[should therefore be encouraged]],}} ideally together with the other habits that keep clothes in use for longer.
map.no: {{On balance, [[it would appear that]]}} the solution lies in producing less, not in the second-hand shop. Buying used clothes is popular for good reasons and does some good, but it cannot absorb the flood of cheap garments, and swaps or repairs only help with clothes that already exist. {{Real change [[will only be achieved]]}} when the industry changes course.
map.partly: {{On balance, [[it would appear that]]}} second-hand shopping is a valuable part of the solution, but only one part. Young people have good reasons to choose it, and every used garment reduces the demand for new ones a little. {{Its limits make it clear that clothes [[should also be bought]]}} less often, looked after well and passed on when they are no longer worn.

options.label: Give a final verdict

map.yes: In conclusion, second-hand shopping is a pleasant trend, but in the end it changes very little. Young people may enjoy flea markets and resale apps, and some of them may even buy fewer new clothes as a result. Fast fashion, however, can only be stopped by the industry itself, never by the choices of individual consumers, so there is little point in encouraging second-hand shopping at all.
map.no: In conclusion, second-hand shopping is clearly the best answer to fast fashion. Young people already love flea markets and resale apps, and every used garment they buy means one new garment less. If enough of them buy used clothes instead of new ones, nothing else needs to change, and the problem will solve itself within a few years.
map.partly: In conclusion, second-hand shopping is clearly the best answer to fast fashion. Young people already love flea markets and resale apps, and every used garment they buy means one new garment less. If enough of them buy used clothes instead of new ones, nothing else needs to change, and the problem will solve itself within a few years.

options.reject: This conclusion argues the opposite of our thesis. A conclusion sums up the position the essay has defended; a sudden change of mind makes the whole essay unconvincing.
options.rejectDe: Der Schluss vertritt plötzlich die Gegenposition zu unserer These. Das macht das ganze Essay unglaubwürdig.

steps.q: Now that the essay is finished, which title do we choose?
steps.de: Zuletzt wählen wir den Titel für unser Essay.
steps.own: Factual and to the point: the title names the topic and fits our position.
steps.ownDe: Sachlich: Der Titel nennt das Thema und passt zu unserer Position.

options.label: State the position
options.why: A short statement title tells the reader the topic and the position at once.

map.yes: Second-hand clothing: the best answer to fast fashion
map.no: Why second-hand shopping cannot stop fast fashion
map.partly: Second-hand shopping: part of the answer to fast fashion

options.label: Name the background
options.why: Factual and serious: it names the topic and the problem behind the essay question.
options.text: Second-hand clothing in a fast-fashion age

options.label: Topic and angle
options.why: Names the topic first and then the angle of the essay.

map.yes: Fast fashion and the case for second-hand
map.no: Fast fashion: a problem consumers cannot solve alone
map.partly: Fast fashion and the limits of second-hand shopping

checks.en: A factual title that states the topic (a statement, not a question)
The introduction ends with a thesis statement that shows our position
All three content points: why second-hand is popular, its limits, other options for consumers
Five paragraphs; each body paragraph opens with a topic sentence linking back to what came before
Impersonal style (our focus): passive and ‘It is …’ instead of ‘I think’; no ‘you’, no contractions
The conclusion picks up the thesis and all three body paragraphs, without new arguments

teacher.aim: Die Klasse baut gemeinsam ein Essay nach SRDP-Standard zur Frage, ob Secondhand die Antwort auf Fast Fashion ist. Fokus: unpersönliche Formulierungen statt I/you, also It- und There-Einleitungen (It could be argued that …, There is a real danger that …) und Passiv mit Modalverb (… should be encouraged).
teacher.prep: A/B/C/D-Karten austeilen, eine Garnitur pro Person (ohne Karten: 1–4 Finger, die Tasten 1–4 wählen wie A–D). Beamer im Vollbild. Die Aufgabe am Beamer enthält alles Nötige. Im Gerüst-Modus den eingebauten Timer nutzen: 5 min für Einleitung und Schluss, 8 min pro Body Paragraph.
teacher.heft: Neue Seite: Datum (rechts), „Essay“ als Überschrift, darunter 2 Zeilen für den Titel frei lassen (der Titel kommt zuletzt). Fünf Absätze, jeder beginnt nach einer Leerzeile; am Rand steht Intro, Body 1, Body 2, Body 3, Conclusion. Unpersönliche Formulierungen grün unterstreichen.
teacher.flow: Volltext (Doppelstunde, 100 min): 5 min Aufgabe lesen und Position wählen, dann 6 Entscheidungen (fünf Absätze, zuletzt der Titel) à ca. 2–3 min, Abschreiben ca. 45 min, 5 min Checkliste. Gerüst (Doppelstunde, 100 min): 3 min Aufgabe und Position; pro Absatz 2 min Abstimmung, dann eigenes Schreiben (Einleitung und Schluss je 5 min, Body Paragraphs je 8 min) und 2 min Vergleich mit dem Modell; am Ende 2 min Titel und 4 min Checkliste. Wird die Zeit knapp, Schluss und Titel als Hausübung.
teacher.traps: Body 1 C (LSA): cheaper as statt than, what statt which, land in statt end up in. Body 2 A (CC): Der Absatz weicht vom Topic Sentence ab: Nach einem Beispiel für die Grenzen geht es wieder um die Beliebtheit von Secondhand (Apps, Flohmärkte, Vintage, Preise). Body 3 B (TA): Der Absatz beschreibt Tauschbörsen, Reparaturcafés und Verleih nur, statt sie zu bewerten (Operator „evaluate“). Conclusion C (CC): Der Schluss vertritt plötzlich die Gegenposition zur eigenen These. Kürzel: TA = Erfüllung der Aufgabenstellung, CC = Kohärenz und Kohäsion, LSR = Spektrum sprachlicher Mittel, LSA = Sprachrichtigkeit.
teacher.notes: Das Essay hat fünf Absätze (Einleitung, drei Hauptteile, Schluss) und wie bei der SRDP eine Länge: ca. 400 Wörter. Jede Entscheidung ist ein ganzer Absatz; Body 2 nimmt in den gültigen Optionen einen Einwand auf und antwortet darauf. Keine Marken nennen und niemanden für den Kauf billiger Kleidung beschämen; nicht thematisieren, wer sich was leisten kann. Die erste Entscheidung (Position yes / no / partly) bestimmt Thesis, Bewertungen und Schluss. Das Essay kommt ohne Statistiken aus: Die Argumente beruhen auf allgemein bekannten Zusammenhängen (Export gebrauchter Kleidung, kurze Lebensdauer billiger Ware). Wer Zahlen ergänzen will, recherchiert sie mit Quelle. Zu Body 3, Option C: Die EU verbietet großen Unternehmen seit Juli 2026, unverkaufte Kleidung und Schuhe zu vernichten, und verpflichtet die Mitgliedstaaten zu Herstellerverantwortung für Textilien. Differenzierung: Schnelle formen im Gerüst-Modus einen eigenen „I think“-Satz in eine unpersönliche Formulierung um. Hausübung: zweite Fassung mit einer anderen Position.
